claims.text: Oxidation resistance in multiprincipal-element alloys is governed by formation of a stable, adherent oxide layer.
Material integrity in harsh high-temperature environments is governed by formation of a stable, adherent oxide layer.
Alloy microstructure influences formation of the stable, adherent oxide layer.
Alloy composition influences formation of the stable, adherent oxide layer.
The distribution and segregation of alloying elements at grain boundaries and surfaces particularly influence oxide-layer formation.
Interaction between alloying elements and oxygen forms a stable, adherent oxide layer.
Optimizing microstructure and composition improves oxidation resistance.
Optimizing microstructure and composition improves material integrity.
Optimized microstructure and composition produce a thinner oxide layer relative to the baseline.
Optimized microstructure and composition improve oxide-scale adhesion relative to the baseline.
Optimized microstructure and composition enhance mechanical properties relative to the baseline.
The proposed governing behavior applies over 500–1000 °C in air or oxygen and under stresses of 0–100 MPa.
Traditional alloy-design methods may be ineffective for multiprincipal-element alloys.
In-situ transmission electron microscopy can reveal oxidation processes, microstructural changes, and elemental segregation in real time under the proposed comparison.
